description: Toy Box Friends G2-11 (grade 2): thirds are three equal parts of one whole; three thirds make the whole; more equal parts means smaller parts; compare parts only when the wholes are the same size.

youtube.title: Pizza Party Thirds! Equal Parts for Kids | Halves, Thirds, Fourths | Toy Box Friends
youtube.description:
One pizza, three hungry friends! Robo, Cat and Bear learn that thirds are three EQUAL parts of one whole. Cat's Fair-Share Scanner stacks the slices to check them, Bear eats one third so we can see two thirds left, and three thirds make the whole pizza again. We cut a flatbread into tall strips and flat strips (both are thirds), line up a half, a third and a fourth (more parts, smaller parts), and catch Robo's Same Size Whole mistake: a half of a tiny pizza is NOT bigger than a third of a giant one. Ends with a Fair Share or Not? challenge and a quiz.

For second graders (CCSS 2.G.A.3: partition circles and rectangles into halves, thirds and fourths).

Try at home: draw a big Y on a paper circle and ask a grown-up to cut along it (grown-ups do the cutting). Stack the three slices: do they match? Then colour one third, then two thirds.

do.text: Pizza Party Thirds
Pizza party! One yummy pizza and three hungry friends.
I am SO hungry. Can we share it?
Let's stand it on the pizza board, so we can all see.
One cut, straight down the middle. Two pieces!
Two pieces... but there are three of us.
Oops! I'll cut it again. Now there are three pieces.
One piece is huge, and two are tiny. Three pieces, but not fair shares.
So how do we share one pizza fairly with three friends?
First, a quick look back. Here is one whole pizza.
whole
The whole is everything we started with.
Cut it into two equal parts, and each part is one half.
half
Equal? Let me check with my Fair-Share Scanner.
They match exactly. Equal parts are the same size.
equal parts = same size
Equal parts make fair shares. Nobody gets less.
fair share
But two halves only work for two friends. We have three.
Let's try my three-piece cut again. Is it fair?
Is this fair?
Scanner time. I'll put a small piece on the big one.
It doesn't cover it. The big piece is a half. The small ones are fourths.
Three parts, but not equal. So they are not thirds.
Now the fair cut. Three cuts from the middle, like the letter Y.
Draw a big Y in the air!
Three slices. Let's scan them. Slice two goes on slice one.
A perfect match! And slice three matches too.
Three equal parts of one whole are called thirds.
3 equal parts = thirds
Each part is one third of the pizza.
one third
Fun fact! The word fraction comes from a Latin word that means to break.
Thirds work for long shapes too. Here is a flatbread.
Two cuts, the same distance apart, make three equal strips.
Each strip is one third of the flatbread.
one third

scenes.title: One third, two thirds, three thirds

do.text: Let's count the thirds. Tap each slice with me.
1 third
One third.
2 thirds
Two thirds.
3 thirds
Three thirds. That's the whole pizza.
May I have one third, please?
Bear took one third. How much pizza is left?
How much is left?
Two thirds are left. One, two.
2 thirds left
Yum! Wait, I'll save mine for later.
Let's push the slice back. Three thirds make one whole pizza again!
3 thirds = 1 whole
Three the same? That's thirds! All three back? That's whole!
Same with the flatbread. Three thirds fill the whole thing.
Here are two flatbreads, exactly the same size.
This one has tall strips. That one has flat strips.
They look different, so they can't both be thirds. Right?
Let's check. I'll cut one tall strip into three little squares.
The squares cover one flat strip exactly. Same amount, different shape.
same amount, different shape
So both flatbreads are cut into thirds. Three equal parts each!
Some pizza shops cut round pizzas into little squares. It's called a party cut.
Knock knock! Look who is here. Pig wants to join the party!
Now there are four friends. We need fourths: four equal parts.
If we cut a pizza into four, will each slice be bigger or smaller?
Bigger or smaller?
Three pizzas, all the same size. Halves, thirds and fourths.
One slice from each pizza slides up so we can compare.
The half is biggest. Then the third. The fourth is smallest.
More equal parts means smaller parts.
More parts, smaller parts
But why? The same pizza is shared by more friends.
One fourth for Pig. Four friends, four equal parts.
A trick! Here is a tiny snack pizza and a giant party pizza.
I take one half of the tiny pizza.
And I take one third of the giant pizza.
A half is bigger than a third, so I win!
Who has more?
My third is much bigger. Your whole pizza was tiny.
A half is bigger than a third only when the wholes are the same size.
Same size whole, then compare
Same whole, then compare. Got it!
Clap along! Three the same?
That's thirds!
All three back?
That's whole!
More parts?
Smaller parts!
Three the same? That's thirds! All three back? That's whole!
Challenge time! Four pictures. Is each one fair, and what is it?
Picture A. A circle in three slices. Thirds?
Yes! Three equal slices are thirds.
Picture B. A rectangle in three parts. Thirds?
No. One part is wider, so they are not equal. Not thirds.
Picture C. One part is shaded. Is that one third?
No! Count all the equal parts. There are four, so it's one fourth.
4 equal parts: one fourth
Picture D. Three equal strips, two are shaded.
That's two thirds. Checked and fair!
two thirds
You found the fair shares. Great checking!
Quiz time! How many thirds make one whole pizza?
Three thirds make one whole.
Bear ate one third. How much is left?
Two thirds are left.
two thirds
Which is bigger, one half or one third of the same pizza?
One half. Fewer parts means bigger parts.
A sandwich is cut into three pieces, but one is bigger. Thirds?
No. Thirds must be equal.
Is a third of a giant pizza the same as a third of a tiny pizza?
No! The wholes are different sizes.
Let's remember. Three equal parts are thirds. Three thirds make one whole.
More parts means smaller parts. And compare only with same-size wholes.
Try it at home! Draw a Y on a paper circle. A grown-up does the cutting.
Grown-ups do the cutting
Then stack your slices to check. Checked and fair!
Bye, friends! Enjoy your fair share!
